title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
author: Aaron C. Davis
content:
In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the
Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup
with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records
reviewed by ProPublica.

The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a
firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a
largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in
private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories
that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for
defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company,
based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced
that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the
venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was
elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.

A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian,
but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.

The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has
made in a recent lending spree.

According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a
dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and
potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and
other equipment.

The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of
munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the
factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.

The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the
company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing
guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials
said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling
defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to,
essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.

Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its
ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.

The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both
chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new
oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the
Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and
others who work in the administration or have ties to it.  

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his
elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing.
ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding [nearly $40
million to one company to screen for
Ebola](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-sons-xwell-xprestest-
government-contracts) and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how [a
White House aide intervened](https://www.propublica.org/article/donald-trump-
jr-vulcan-deal-white-house) to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to
Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital
invested in it.

![A man signs the guest book at the New York Stock Exchange while several
other individuals in business attire — including Donald Trump Jr. — look
on.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2224717937.jpg?w=2560)Omeed Malik, founder
of 1789 Capital, center, signs the guest book on the floor of the New York
Stock Exchange in 2025 as Donald Trump Jr. looks on. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg
via Getty Images

Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789
lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company
receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or
political connections play absolutely no role in the Department's funding
decisions."

A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being
in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion.
The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under
discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other
companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.

In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government
contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian.
“Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic
industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply
chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to
strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns
for our investors."  

Trump Jr.'s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian
being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company's
operations. "Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and
investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public
office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence
government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his
personal business interests," his lawyer said.

Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.

In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive
investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a
conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.

1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year.
That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor
Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand
its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new
factory in Arizona.

This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy,
which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO
became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half
million dollars, campaign filings show.  

1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of
financing that included participation from institutional investment managers.
“This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in [a LinkedIn
post](https://lnkd.in/p/g56_vtvF) about the funding round.

It’s unclear when the Pentagon began considering Hadrian for the loan. But
defense documents cite the August funding round that Trump Jr.’s firm was part
of. It’s also not clear if the White House played any role in Hadrian’s being
considered, though defense documents about the deal mention the “White House
and DoW leadership’s expressed need for advanced manufacturing” — which
Hadrian specializes in.

In response to questions to the White House, an administration official said
Hadrian reached out to the Pentagon proposing a loan and that “It is at an
extremely early stage.” (The documents ProPublica reviewed show specific terms
being considered by the Pentagon for the loan and discussions of its merits
and risks.)

At the March ribbon cutting for the first of three factories to be built for
submarine parts and systems for the Navy, Hadrian’s Australian-born founder,
Chris Power, promised a radical change to defense manufacturing. “The number-
one problem that the Navy's identified is we can't find enough skilled
workers, so we have to automate our way out of this problem,” [he told
reporters](https://www.defenseone.com/defense-systems/2026/03/navy-
bets-900m-automated-factories-boost-submarine-production/412290/). The factory
will be run on its artificial intelligence software, called Opus, which Power
said would make his production line more efficient and nimble.

The Navy “can’t hire enough people and the primes can’t hire enough people
because there aren’t enough trained people to do it,” he said, referring to
major defense contractors. “We need to automate and have people running
multiple robots in a new way of doing things versus replacing jobs.”

Venture capital firms are betting heavily that the marriage of AI and robotics
will lead to major upheaval in manufacturing sectors, investing $33 billion —
more than all of last year — in just the first half of 2026, according to data
from PitchBook.

When it comes to defense contracting, analysts have said that they expect only
a handful of companies will succeed, with a wave of consolidations to follow.
A mega Defense Department contract for Hadrian could position it as just such
a winner — even as the company has shared few details publicly about what its
AI-powered factories have so far been able to produce. In testimony before
Congress last year, Power said only that the company had successfully
fabricated parts for “missile systems, fighter jets, spacecraft and naval
vessels.”  
  
Power started the company in 2020, saying he moved to the U.S. with just
$6,000 and began cold-calling manufacturers looking to develop an idea to
understand their operations and probe for bottlenecks. Much of the aerospace
and defense industries, he found, relied on small shops with experts who were
close to retirement. The solution, he decided, was automation.

Hadrian executives [told
Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/amyfeldman/2024/08/15/this-high-tech-
factory-makes-parts-for-rockets-and-fighter-jets-10-times-faster-hadrian-
chris-power/) in 2024 that the company spent its first two years trying to
replicate components for two companies using its automation software in a
small demonstration factory in California. It never named the companies or
said which components it was able to replicate. It hired employees away from
Elon Musk companies SpaceX and Tesla. It also hired employees from defense
contractors Anduril, Raytheon and Palantir. Hadrian has also drawn investments
from high-profile Silicon Valley funds, including Andreessen Horowitz and
Altimeter Capital. The company has not released a recent employee count, but
outside estimates put it at a few hundred.

This year, Hadrian has announced openings of new plants faster than outside
analysts have been able to assess how well its operations are working. Mesa,
Arizona, officials celebrated opening the company’s third factory in January.
The ribbon cutting for its fourth, in Alabama for the Navy, took place in
March, with Hadrian saying full production would begin in a couple of years.

![A crowd of people walks past a life-size model of a submarine beneath a
large American flag during a ribbon-cutting event in a new production
facility.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/AP26079744907558.jpg)A submarine model is displayed
beneath a large U.S. flag during a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the Hadrian
submarine component facility in Barton, Alabama, in March. Dan Busey/The
TimesDaily via AP

A multibillion-dollar investment in Hadrian could push the Pentagon’s Office
of Strategic Capital far beyond the purpose for which it was approved and
funded by Congress, some former defense officials said.

The office was created during the Biden administration to fill holes in the
country’s industrial base so that the U.S. can stop relying on China, its top
rival, to equip its own military. Under Trump, the lending unit has greatly
expanded and focused on issuing loans to private companies to develop
production of rare earth minerals and other technologies that have both
commercial and military applications. That need has been elevated as the
president’s tariff wars have heightened concerns that China could cut off the
flow of critical minerals needed to produce high-tech weapons. The firms
receiving loans generally make their money by supplying both defense
contractors and other private-sector businesses.

But the idea of loaning money to Hadrian in hopes that it grows to become a
major source of military munitions has sparked concerns within the Pentagon
that the company would become reliant largely on the federal government.

When Congress created the Office of Strategic Capital, it included language
prohibiting the OSC from making loans for projects with only military
applications. A Pentagon document describing the proposed Hadrian loan
indicates that the firm’s new factories would expand the U.S. capability to
manufacture munitions and precision components for military use. The document
states that Hadrian factories could “pivot rapidly to commercial
applications.”

The former defense officials said the U.S. government might face allegations
that it would be giving a distinct advantage to Hadrian over potential
competitors. Other businesses could challenge whether the company is winning
bids or subcontracting work on its merits or so that taxpayers do not lose on
their capital investment.

David Lorch, a political appointee who heads up OSC, would have to sign off on
the loan. Lorch previously worked at Cerberus, the private equity firm founded
by Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg. It’s unclear if Feinberg or others
in the Trump administration would also have to approve the deal because of its
size.  

A former defense official familiar with the OSC said a Hadrian loan of that
magnitude could put the lending unit’s credibility in jeopardy with the
incoming Congress, which would likely have to approve additional funds to
allow it to continue issuing new loans.

“OSC is clearly a powerful tool to advance national security. But its ability
to invest and access to long-term funding are tenuous,” the official said.
“Some senior leaders seemingly want to use it as a pot of money for deals that
exceed its mandate.”

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/GettyImages-2273875370_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1)
**The White House Intervened to Get a $620 Million Deal for a Company Tied to
Donald Trump Jr.** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/donald-trump-jr-
vulcan-deal-white-house)

In the past, Trump Jr. and his firm have said he does not discuss the
companies he invests in with federal officials. In his public comments, he has
shown a personal interest in [defense tech](https://rumble.com/v6z4x50-the-
warrior-ethos-and-americas-mission-interview-with-harpoon-ventures-foun.html)
and has [criticized
cronyism](https://open.spotify.com/episode/4btTjAZi2SmNQVEI2eanac) in defense
spending.

The Office of Strategic Capital was also behind the decision to give hundreds
of millions of dollars in loans to Vulcan Elements just months after Trump
Jr.’s venture firm invested in the company.

Of the dozens of companies the Pentagon was considering funding at the time,
Vulcan’s was the only deal brought forward by a top aide to the president,
[ProPublica previously reported](https://www.propublica.org/article/donald-
trump-jr-vulcan-deal-white-house). After defense officials got the White House
request, they asked Pentagon staff to move at an unusually rapid pace, and
staff worked late nights and with little sleep to get the loan through in a
matter of weeks.

The Pentagon denied any preferential treatment, and Trump Jr. said he played
no role in the deal.
